chapter_theme: அருள், compassion extended to all living beings, is the highest wealth and the basis of other virtue. The chapter promises its possessor freedom from suffering and denies its lack any recovery, then closes by showing how it can be cultivated.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of அருள் (241-242), the absence of suffering in both worlds for those who have it (243-245), the faults of those without it (246-249), and how it is brought about (250).

241.reading: The wealth of அருள் is the wealth among wealths, because the wealth of goods is found even among the base.
241.nuance: The argument is about distribution: what the worst can have can't be the best thing. It doesn't say goods are bad, and 247 will concede how much depends on them.

242.reading: Examine by sound means and hold to அருள்; however many ways you investigate, that alone is the companion.
242.nuance: Compassion here is what inquiry concludes, not an alternative to it. Parimelazhagar reads பல்லாற்றால் as the competing religious systems, which disagree on means of knowledge and objects but converge here. The verse itself mentions no sects, so this ecumenical reading is his.

positions.position: Mutually opposed schools agree on this one point.
positions.quote: அன்னவாயினும், அருள் துணை என்றற்கண் ஒக்கும் என்பதாம்.

243.reading: Those whose hearts are joined with அருள் will not enter the painful world joined with darkness.
243.nuance: அருள் and இருள் rhyme across the verse, and the same word, சேர்ந்த, joins each to its noun.

positions.position: It is a literal hell, a place in the lower world.
The darkness is ignorance, and the suffering is of this life.
positions.quote: அறியாமை எனும் இருள் சூழ்ந்த துன்ப உலகில்

244.reading: They say that one who sustains living beings and holds to அருள் has no deeds his own life need fear.
244.nuance: Care for other lives removes the fear for one's own. Parimelazhagar takes மன் as making souls eternal, a doctrine not required by the word, and gives a causal link: such a person won't kill, and hence won't go to hell.

245.reading: Those who hold to அருள் have no distress, and the wide rich earth where the wind moves is the witness.
245.nuance: Parimelazhagar's witness is negative: no one has ever seen such a person suffer, so the whole world can testify. Kalaignar instead makes the wind an analogy for அருள் moving the mind. The claim of no distress is bold, and should be read with the reservation of 169.

246.reading: Those who abandon அருள் and carry on doing what should not be done, they say, have parted from பொருள் and forgotten.

positions.position: பொருள் is virtue: they failed to practise it before and have forgotten the suffering they are in as a result.
positions.quote: முன்னும் உறுதிப் பொருளைச் செய்யாது தாம் துன்புறுகின்றமையை மறந்தவர்

positions.position: பொருள் is wealth, and the verse spans lives: lacking அருள் in a former birth, they are now both poor and forgetful.
With no former birth in view, the cruel become poor and forget their duty.

247.reading: As this world is not for those without wealth, that world is not for those without அருள்.
247.nuance: The comparison gets its force from its blunt premise about money, which the verse states as obvious fact. A chapter that opened by belittling goods grants them complete authority over this world.

positions.quote: உயிர்கள்மேல் அருள் இல்லாதார்க்கு வீட்டுலகத்து இன்பம் இல்லை

positions.position: It isn't another world at all: wealth is to the household life as compassion is to the renouncer's life.
positions.quote: கருணை உள்ளம் இல்லாதவர்களின் துறவற வாழ்க்கையும் சிறப்பாக அமையாது.

248.reading: Those without wealth may flower one day; those without அருள் are finished, and it is hard for them to become anything again.
248.nuance: Parimelazhagar sees this as withdrawing the parallel just drawn in 247, since the two lacks aren't alike after all. His addition of 'through fate' to the poor man's state is not in the verse.

249.reading: Virtue done by one without அருள், if examined, is like the muddled person seeing the true reality.
249.nuance: Parimelazhagar concludes that அருள் is the root of all other virtues. That goes beyond the comparison the verse draws, but it is a natural development.

positions.position: Such virtue can occur, as a passing glimpse can, but the person's own lack destroys it.
positions.quote: அருளாதான் இடையே அறஞ்செய்தால் அதனைத் தன் அருளாமையால் தானே அழித்துவிடும்

positions.position: Such people can't practise virtue at all.

250.reading: When you go against those weaker than yourself, think of yourself before those stronger.
250.nuance: The chapter's only instruction on how compassion arises doesn't appeal to a principle: it asks you to remember your own fear. Parimelazhagar calls this the means by which அருள் is born, and extends the weaker to animals too.

links.note: The same formula, செல்வத்துட் செல்வம், crowns different things: அருள் here and hearing in 411. Both can't be 'the' wealth of wealths unless the phrase is a rhetorical form awarded in context, a caution against reading any single chapter as the Kural's ultimate ranking.

247 mentions as an aside that this world is not for the penniless. 751 makes that its full subject: nothing but wealth makes nobodies into somebodies. The section on virtue quietly grants the premise of the section on wealth.

248 says those without அருள் are finished and can't become anything. 250, which Parimelazhagar calls the means of arousing அருள், assumes that the person going against the weak can still acquire it. The verdict is absolute, and the very next step offers a way out.
34 says stainlessness of mind is the whole of virtue and all else is show. 249 makes the same point about compassion: an outwardly right act without it does not count.

Both derive compassion from one's own experience: 250 remembers fear before the strong, and 318 asks how one who knows pain in his own life could inflict it. The Kural's ethics of harm consistently starts from self-knowledge and not from rules.

source_issues: 242: the verse text has நல்லாற்றாள் where Parimelazhagar's gloss reads நல் ஆற்றான். No Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
241: Parimelazhagar's gloss has பவற்றுள்ளும, likely a misprint for பலவற்றுள்ளும.
249: Parimelazhagar's text has a stray character in அறங்கட்கெல்‘ம்.
